modules.title: 1 · Probability models and random variables
modules.summary: Build coherent probability models and translate them into simulated data.

stages.title: Probability models and random variables: research guide
stages.html:
Probability models and random variables

Build coherent probability models and translate them into simulated data.

Probability statements become useful only after the support, conditioning information, and data-generating experiment are explicit.

Workflow. Define a sample space, events, and a coherent distribution before calculating.

Diagnostic: Inspect support, normalization, and conditioning information. The main failure to avoid is probabilities attached to impossible or incomplete events.

stages.title: Probability models intuition lab
stages.note: Set the mixing weight and separation: the two-component model defines one normalized density, and the simulated draws fall exactly under it.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
p = {{p}}; sep = {{sep}}; n = 4000
# model: with prob p draw N(-sep/2,1), else N(+sep/2,1)
z = rng.random(n) < p
x = np.where(z, rng.normal(-sep/2, 1, n), rng.normal(sep/2, 1, n))
grid = np.linspace(-7, 7, 500)
dens = p*stats.norm.pdf(grid, -sep/2, 1) + (1-p)*stats.norm.pdf(grid, sep/2, 1)
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.hist(x, bins=55, density=True, color='#da9100', alpha=0.5, label='simulated draws')
plt.plot(grid, dens, color='#c9c6ac', lw=2, label='model density')
plt.legend(); plt.xlabel('x'); plt.ylabel('density')
plt.title(f'two-component model: p={p:.2f}, separation={sep:.1f}')
model_mean = p*(-sep/2) + (1-p)*(sep/2)
print(f'model mean = {model_mean:.3f}, empirical mean = {x.mean():.3f}')
print(f'density integrates to {np.trapz(dens, grid):.3f} (a coherent model normalizes to 1)')

stages.note: Run the reproducible example, then change one assumption and compare the output.

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n = 40
repetitions = 2000
means = rng.normal(loc=2.0, scale=3.0, size=(repetitions, n)).mean(axis=1)
print(f"Monte Carlo mean: {means.mean():.3f}")
print(f"Monte Carlo SE:   {means.std(ddof=1):.3f}")
print(f"Theory SE:        {3 / np.sqrt(n):.3f}")

modules.title: 2 · Sampling distributions
modules.summary: See estimators as random variables across repeated samples.

stages.title: Sampling distributions: research guide
stages.html:
Sampling distributions

See estimators as random variables across repeated samples.

A sampling distribution answers what would vary if the full sampling process were repeated, not what varies inside one fitted dataset.

Workflow. Use expectations for location and variance for dispersion around the mean.

Diagnostic: Inspect units, existence of moments, and covariance terms. The main failure to avoid is dropping dependence terms or confusing spread with level.

stages.title: Expectation and variance intuition lab
stages.note: Increase n: the wide spread of a single dataset stays fixed, but the sampling distribution of the mean concentrates as sigma/sqrt(n).
stages.template:
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = int({{n}}); reps = 3000
# skewed population: exponential, mean=2, sd=2
samples = rng.exponential(2.0, size=(reps, n))
means = samples.mean(axis=1)
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.hist(samples[0], bins=40, density=True, color='#da9100', alpha=0.35, label='one dataset (raw x)')
plt.hist(means, bins=40, density=True, color='#3b6ea5', alpha=0.6, label='sampling dist of mean')
plt.axvline(2.0, color='#c9c6ac', lw=2, label='population mean')
plt.legend(); plt.xlabel('value'); plt.ylabel('density')
plt.title(f'n={n}: SE(mean)={means.std(ddof=1):.3f} vs theory {2.0/np.sqrt(n):.3f}')
print(f'mean of sample means = {means.mean():.3f} (population mean = 2.000)')
print(f'empirical SE = {means.std(ddof=1):.3f}, sigma/sqrt(n) = {2.0/np.sqrt(n):.3f}')

modules.title: 3 · Estimator properties
modules.summary: Separate bias, variance, consistency, and efficiency.

stages.title: Estimator properties: research guide
stages.html:
Estimator properties

Separate bias, variance, consistency, and efficiency.

Finite-sample bias and asymptotic consistency are different claims; an estimator can trade bias for lower mean-squared error.

Workflow. Connect sample averages to population expectations under stated dependence conditions.

Diagnostic: Inspect sample size, dependence, and moment existence. The main failure to avoid is assuming every average converges regardless of the data process.

stages.title: Law of Large Numbers intuition lab
stages.note: Shrink the sample mean toward zero: at lambda=1 it is unbiased, but for a weak signal an intermediate lambda trades a little bias for lower MSE.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
mu = {{mu}}; lam = {{lam}}; n = 20; reps = 4000
samples = rng.normal(mu, 1.0, size=(reps, n))
xbar = samples.mean(axis=1)
est = lam * xbar                      # shrinkage estimator toward 0
bias = est.mean() - mu; var = est.var(); mse = np.mean((est - mu)**2)
lams = np.linspace(0, 1.2, 60)
mse_curve = [np.mean((L*xbar - mu)**2) for L in lams]
best = lams[int(np.argmin(mse_curve))]
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.plot(lams, mse_curve, color='#c9c6ac', lw=2, label='MSE(lambda)')
plt.axvline(lam, color='#da9100', lw=2, label=f'chosen lambda={lam:.2f}')
plt.scatter([lam], [mse], color='#da9100', zorder=5)
plt.xlabel('shrinkage lambda'); plt.ylabel('MSE'); plt.legend()
plt.title(f'bias={bias:.3f}, var={var:.3f}, MSE={mse:.3f}')
print(f'unbiased mean (lambda=1): MSE={np.mean((xbar-mu)**2):.3f}')
print(f'chosen lambda={lam:.2f}: bias={bias:.3f}, variance={var:.3f}, MSE={mse:.3f}; MSE-optimal lambda approx {best:.2f}')

modules.title: 4 · LLN, CLT, and asymptotic inference
modules.summary: Connect probability limits to usable large-sample uncertainty.

stages.title: LLN, CLT, and asymptotic inference: research guide
stages.html:
LLN, CLT, and asymptotic inference

Connect probability limits to usable large-sample uncertainty.

The LLN supports convergence of averages; the CLT supplies a scaled limiting distribution when its regularity conditions hold.

Workflow. Standardize an estimator and justify its limiting reference distribution.

Diagnostic: Inspect rate, variance, and dependence conditions. The main failure to avoid is normal inference without an applicable asymptotic approximation.

stages.title: Central Limit Theorem intuition lab
stages.note: Raise n: even though the parent is a skewed exponential, the standardized sample mean sqrt(n)(xbar-mu)/sigma flattens into the standard normal.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = int({{n}}); reps = 5000
# skewed parent: exponential, mean=1, sd=1
samples = rng.exponential(1.0, size=(reps, n))
zstat = np.sqrt(n) * (samples.mean(axis=1) - 1.0) / 1.0
grid = np.linspace(-4, 4, 300)
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.hist(zstat, bins=45, density=True, color='#da9100', alpha=0.5, label='sqrt(n)(xbar-mu)/sigma')
plt.plot(grid, stats.norm.pdf(grid), color='#c9c6ac', lw=2, label='N(0,1)')
plt.legend(); plt.xlabel('standardized mean'); plt.ylabel('density')
plt.title(f'CLT from a skewed parent, n={n}')
print(f'n={n}: skew of standardized mean = {stats.skew(zstat):.3f} (shrinks toward 0)')
print(f'empirical variance = {zstat.var():.3f} (approaches 1)')

modules.title: 5 · Monte Carlo and bootstrap
modules.summary: Validate estimators through controlled repetition and defensible resampling.

stages.title: Monte Carlo and bootstrap: research guide
stages.html:
Monte Carlo and bootstrap

Validate estimators through controlled repetition and defensible resampling.

Monte Carlo varies simulated datasets from a known process; bootstrap varies resamples from observed data and must preserve dependence.

Workflow. Repeat a controlled data-generating process and summarize estimator behavior.

Diagnostic: Inspect random seed policy, repetitions, bias, variance, and coverage. The main failure to avoid is a simulation conclusion based on one realization.

stages.title: Monte Carlo experiments intuition lab
stages.note: Adjust the observed sample size and the number of resamples: the bootstrap distribution of the mean recovers a standard error and 95% interval from one dataset alone.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = int({{n}}); B = int({{B}})
# one observed sample from a skewed process (gamma, mean=4)
data = rng.gamma(2.0, 2.0, n)
idx = rng.integers(0, n, size=(B, n))
boot_means = data[idx].mean(axis=1)
lo, hi = np.percentile(boot_means, [2.5, 97.5])
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.hist(boot_means, bins=40, density=True, color='#da9100', alpha=0.55, label='bootstrap means')
plt.axvline(data.mean(), color='#c9c6ac', lw=2, label='observed sample mean')
plt.axvline(lo, color='#3b6ea5', ls='--'); plt.axvline(hi, color='#3b6ea5', ls='--', label='95% CI')
plt.legend(); plt.xlabel('resampled mean'); plt.ylabel('density')
plt.title(f'nonparametric bootstrap: n={n}, B={B}')
print(f'bootstrap SE = {boot_means.std(ddof=1):.3f} vs analytic s/sqrt(n) = {data.std(ddof=1)/np.sqrt(n):.3f}')
print(f'95% percentile CI = [{lo:.3f}, {hi:.3f}]')
